news <- read.csv(here("data", "fake_news_bayesrules.csv"))

news_glm <- glm(type_num ~ title_caps_percent, data = news, family = binomial)
excl_glm <- glm(type_num ~ title_has_excl, data = news, family = binomial)
b <- unname(coef(news_glm))

## Where we're going

So far, our response variable has always been **quantitative**. Today the
response is **binary** (yes/no, success/failure), so we need a new model:
**logistic regression**.

## Data: fake news

150 news articles, some real and some fake. Our goal is to explain `type`
using features of the article.

-   `type`: "real" or "fake"; `type_num`: 0 (real) or 1 (fake)
-   `title_words`: number of words in the title
-   `title_has_excl`: whether the title has an exclamation point
-   `title_caps_percent`: percent of the title in capital letters

A "success" ($Y = 1$) is a _____________ article. Always check how your response
is coded before modeling!

**Q1.** Before we do anything else, how do you think `title_has_excl` and `title_caps_percent` are related to `type_num`?

\vspace{2in}

## Probability and odds

If $\pi$ is the probability of an event, the **odds** of the event are

$$\text{odds} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} = \frac{P(\text{event})}{P(\text{not event})} \qquad\qquad \pi = \frac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$$

| Probability $\pi$ | Odds $\pi/(1-\pi)$ | How we'd say it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 0.5 | 1 | "even odds" |
| 0.75 | 3 | "3 to 1" |
| 0.2 | 0.25 | "1 to 4" |

Probabilities are between 0 and 1; odds are between 0 and $\infty$.


## Example: exclamation points

```{r}
table(news$title_has_excl, news$type) |>
  addmargins() |>
  knitr::kable()
```

| | Title has exclamation | No exclamation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $P(\text{fake})$ | $16/18 = 0.889$ | ________________________ |
| $\text{Odds}(\text{fake})$ | $16/2 = 8$ | ________________________ |

Shortcut: from a table, odds = (number of successes) / (number of failures).

The **odds ratio** compares the odds in two groups:

$$OR = \frac{\text{Odds}(\text{fake} \mid \text{exclamation})}{\text{Odds}(\text{fake} \mid \text{no exclamation})} = \frac{8}{\underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}} = 16$$

**Interpretation:** The odds of being fake are 16 times as high for articles
with an exclamation point in the title as for articles without one.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

An odds ratio is **not** a ratio of probabilities. It is *not* correct to say
that articles with an exclamation point are "16 times as likely" to be fake:
the ratio of probabilities is only about 2.67.
:::

## Why not linear regression?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.4
lm_fit <- lm(type_num ~ title_caps_percent, data = news)

p_lm <- gf_jitter(type_num ~ title_caps_percent, data = news, width = 0.2, height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_lm(color = "#f15a31") |>
  gf_labs(y = "Fake = 1", title = "Linear regression")
p_glm <- gf_jitter(type_num ~ title_caps_percent, data = news, width = 0.2, height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = FALSE, color = "#f15a31") |>
  gf_labs(y = "Fake = 1", title = "Logistic regression")
p_lm + p_glm
```

A line keeps going forever, so it predicts "probabilities" outside of
$[0, 1]$: the linear model predicts
`r f2(predict(lm_fit, data.frame(title_caps_percent = max(news$title_caps_percent))))`
for the title with the most capital letters
(`r max(news$title_caps_percent)`%). Logistic regression gives an S-shaped
curve that stays between 0 and 1.

## The logistic regression model

$$\log\left(\frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p$$

where $\pi(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid x)$. The left side is called the **log-odds** or
the **logit**. It can be any number, so it's OK for the right side to be a
line.

| Scale | Formula | Range | Linear in the $x$'s? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Probability | $\pi$ | 0 to 1 | ________ |
| Odds | $\pi / (1 - \pi)$ | 0 to $\infty$ | ________ |
| Log-odds | $\log(\pi / (1 - \pi))$ | $-\infty$ to $\infty$ | ________ |

## Fitting the model in R

```{r}
#| echo: true
news_glm <- glm(type_num ~ title_caps_percent, data = news, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
kable_coef(news_glm, terms = c("Intercept", "title_caps_percent"))
```

$$\widehat\eta = \log\left(\frac{\widehat\pi(x)}{1-\widehat\pi(x)}\right) = `r f3(b[1])` + `r f3(b[2])` x$$

where $x$ is `title_caps_percent`. 

## Interpreting the slope

$\widehat\beta_1 = `r f3(b[2])`$ is the change in the **log-odds** for a
1-unit increase in $x$. To get to the odds scale, exponentiate:

$$\widehat{\text{odds}}(x) = e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}(x+1)}{\widehat{\text{odds}}(x)} = \frac{e^{\widehat\beta_0} e^{\widehat\beta_1 (x+1)}}{e^{\widehat\beta_0} e^{\widehat\beta_1 x}} = e^{\widehat\beta_1}$$

So $e^{\widehat\beta_1}$ is an **odds ratio**. Here,
$e^{`r f3(b[2])`} \approx `r f3(exp(b[2]))`$:

> For each additional percentage point of capital letters in the title, the
> __________ of the article being fake __________________ by about `r f2(exp(b[2]))`
> (an increase of about ______________________________).

For a $c$-unit increase in $x$, the odds are multiplied by $e^{c\widehat\beta_1}$.

What happens to the odds of fake news if the percent of capital letters increases by 10 percentage points? 

> The odds ___________________________ by _________________________________

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistakes

-   $\widehat\beta_1$ is **not** the change in the probability. In logistic
    regression, the change in probability for a 1-unit increase in $x$
    depends on $x$.
-   $e^{\widehat\beta_1}$ **multiplies** the odds; it is not added to them.
-   $e^{\widehat\beta_1}$ multiplies the **odds**, not the probability.
:::

## From log-odds to probability

What's the estimated probability that an article with **20%** capital letters
in the title is fake? Work from the inside out:

```{r}
eta20 <- b[1] + b[2] * 20
```

1.  **Log-odds:** $\widehat\eta = `r f3(b[1])` + `r f3(b[2])`(20) = `r f3(eta20)`$
2.  **Odds:** $\widehat\omega = e^{\widehat\eta} = e^{`r f3(eta20)`} = `r f2(exp(eta20))`$
3.  **Probability:** $\widehat\pi = \dfrac{\widehat\omega}{1 + \widehat\omega} = \dfrac{e^{\widehat\eta}}{1 + e^{\widehat\eta}} = \dfrac{`r f2(exp(eta20))`}{1 + `r f2(exp(eta20))`} = `r f3(exp(eta20) / (1 + exp(eta20)))`$

The intercept works the same way: at $x = 0$, the log-odds are
___________________, the odds are ___________________, and the
probability is ___________________.

**In R**, `predict()` does this for you, but by default it gives the
**log-odds**. Use `type = "response"` to get probabilities:

```{r}
#| echo: true
predict(news_glm, newdata = data.frame(title_caps_percent = 20))
predict(news_glm, newdata = data.frame(title_caps_percent = 20), type = "response")
```

*Note:* The first line of output (without type = "response") is on which scale? _____________________

## The fitted model on three scales

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
tibble(x = seq(0, 60, by = 0.5),
       `1. log-odds` = b[1] + b[2] * x,
       `2. odds` = exp(`1. log-odds`),
       `3. probability` = `2. odds` / (1 + `2. odds`)) |>
  pivot_longer(-x) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#003300", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(name), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "title_caps_percent", y = "")
```

**Q3.** Describe the shape of the fitted model on each of the three scales. Why does the probability curve flatten out near 1?

\vspace{2in}

## Moving between the three scales

| From | To | Formula | In R |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| log-odds $\eta$ | odds | $e^{\eta}$ | `exp(eta)` |
| odds | probability | $\dfrac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$ | `odds / (1 + odds)` |
| log-odds $\eta$ | probability | $\dfrac{e^{\eta}}{1 + e^{\eta}}$ | `exp(eta) / (1 + exp(eta))` |
| probability $\pi$ | odds | $\dfrac{\pi}{1 - \pi}$ | `p / (1 - p)` |
| odds | log-odds | $\log(\text{odds})$ | `log(odds)` |


## A binary predictor gives back the odds ratio

```{r}
#| echo: true
excl_glm <- glm(type_num ~ title_has_excl, data = news, family = binomial)
exp(coef(excl_glm))
```

-   $e^{\widehat\beta_1} = `r round(exp(coef(excl_glm))[2], 1)`$ is exactly the
    odds ratio we computed from the table.

## Interpretation templates

| Quantity | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| $\widehat\beta_j$ | Change in the log-odds of success for a 1-unit increase in $x_j$, holding other predictors constant |
| $e^{\widehat\beta_j}$, quantitative $x_j$ | For a 1-unit increase in $x_j$, the odds of success are multiplied by $e^{\widehat\beta_j}$, holding other predictors constant |
| $e^{\widehat\beta_j}$, indicator $x_j$ | The odds of success are $e^{\widehat\beta_j}$ times as high for the indicated group as for the reference group, holding other predictors constant |
| $e^{\widehat\beta_0}$ | The odds of success when all predictors equal 0 (or for the reference group) |

## R function reference

| Function | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `table(x, y) |> addmargins()` | Two-way table with row and column totals |
| `glm(y ~ x, data, family = binomial)` | Fit a binary logistic regression model |
| `coef(model)`, `exp(coef(model))` | Coefficients on the log-odds scale; odds ratios |
| `summary(model)` | Model summary and Wald tests |
| `predict(model, newdata)` | Predictions on the log-odds scale |
| `predict(model, newdata, type = "response")` | Predictions on the probability scale |
